cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: Xenia was the sacred code of hospitality between guest and host, protected by Zeus Xenios

cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: A good host provided food, drink, a bath, rest and a gift before asking the guest's identity

cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: A good guest showed respect, did not outstay their welcome and did not make excessive demands

cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: The Phaeacians (King Alcinous and Queen Arete) demonstrate ideal xenia — they host Odysseus generously

cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: The Cyclops Polyphemus violates xenia completely — he eats his guests instead of feeding them

cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: The suitors in Odysseus's palace abuse xenia by consuming his resources and courting his wife

cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: Eumaeus the swineherd shows perfect xenia despite his poverty — he welcomes the disguised Odysseus warmly

cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: Violating xenia brought divine punishment — the suitors are killed for their abuse of hospitality

cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: Xenia was essential for travel and trade in a world without hotels or formal diplomacy

cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: The exchange of gifts between host and guest created lasting bonds of mutual obligation

cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: Nestor and Menelaus both show proper xenia to Telemachus during his journey

cards.front: Recall a key point about Xenia (Hospitality)
cards.back: Xenia reflected the Greek belief that strangers might be gods in disguise (as in the myth of Baucis and Philemon)
